title: Shell Basics and Unix Utilities
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter answers: what is the shell, and why is it worth learning a set of decades-old text-processing commands when R and Python can do the same computations? It assumes only that you can open a terminal; it does not reproduce the syntax of individual commands (`cd`, `ls`, `ssh`, redirection) — the course assigns an external tutorial for that — but it does explain, and show in use, the three ways commands talk to each other, a handful of worked examples built from `cut`, `grep`, `sed`, `xargs` and shell functions, and the basics of regular expressions as used from the shell. ## The shell as an interface to Unix The shell is the interface between you and a UNIX-style operating system. When you open a terminal window you are talking to a shell, and from it you run commands such as `cp`, `ls`, `grep`, or start other programs. "UNIX" here means the family of operating systems descending from the UNIX system built at AT&T Bell Labs in the 1970s — MacOS and the various Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Debian, CentOS, Fedora) among them. There are several shells (`sh`, `bash`, `zsh`, `csh`, `tcsh`, `ksh`); the course works in `bash`, which is the common shell on Linux, was the default on MacOS until Catalina (`zsh`, very similar to `bash`, is now the default), and is what runs on the department's SCF machines and the campus cluster (Savio). Any of bash-on-Linux, the older bash shipped on MacOS, or zsh will do for the course's purposes. Windows' PowerShell and the old `cmd.exe` provide a command line but not a UNIX-based one, and are not covered here. A recurring practical annoyance: the UNIX utilities differ slightly between Linux and MacOS, usually in which command-line options are accepted — for example `ls --all` works on Linux but not on MacOS. Several of the worked examples below note where this bites. ## Why the shell, still UNIX shell commands are each built to do one specific task well and fast. They are modular and composable — you build complicated operations by chaining simple ones together — and although the tools are decades old, that composability is exactly why the shell remains central to reproducible scientific computing: it lets you automate a workflow, and once learned, it is faster to type than the equivalent would be in a general-purpose language. One consequence worth internalizing before the examples: most commands that operate on the *content* of a file (as opposed to commands like `ls` or `cd` that operate on the filesystem) work only on text files, and they work on it line by line. A file has to be plain text for `cut`, `grep`, `sed` and friends to be useful on it directly. ## Three ways to pass information between commands The worked examples below lean on three plumbing mechanisms, and it is worth naming them before seeing them combined: - **Piping** (`|`) passes information from one command to another via the first command's `stdout` becoming the second command's `stdin`. - **Command substitution** (`$(...)`) runs a command and captures its output as a string — either to store in a variable, or inline, as a temporary way to pass one command's output as an argument to another. - **Redirection** (`>` and `>>`) sends a command's output into a file, overwriting or appending. The subtlety that trips people up is that a command can accept input either as a named FILE argument or from `stdin`, and these are not interchangeable: a command reading from `stdin` has no idea what file, if any, that text came from. Mission 3 below is built entirely around this distinction. ## Worked examples The examples work on data files distributed with the course (`coop.txt`, a fixed-width weather station file; `cpds.csv`; `RTADataSub.csv`, a subset of Australian freeway travel-time data from a Kaggle competition) and on the course's own `.qmd` source files. ### Mission 1 — profile a column without loading the file Suppose you want the number of weather stations per state, from `coop.txt`, and the state code sits in a fixed byte range of each line: ```bash gzip -cd coop.txt.gz | less # peek at the compressed file gunzip coop.txt.gz cut -b50-70 coop.txt | less # a wider window to spot the field cut -b60-61 coop.txt | uniq # uniq only collapses *adjacent* repeats cut -b60-61 coop.txt | sort | uniq # sort first to collapse all repeats cut -b60-61 coop.txt | sort | uniq -c # add counts ## all in one line, with no change to the original file: gzip -cd coop.txt.gz | cut -b60-61 coop.txt | sort | uniq -c ``` This could be done in R or Python, but that would mean starting the interpreter and reading the whole file into memory; the shell version streams the data through each command line by line and never materializes it as a data frame. Figuring out that the state code lives in bytes 60–61 was done here by eye — the fifth exercise below asks you to automate that instead. ### Mission 2 — count the fields in a CSV, programmatically ```bash tail -n 1 cpds.csv | grep -o ',' | wc -l nfields=$(tail -n 1 cpds.csv | grep -o ',' | wc -l) nfields=$((${nfields}+1)) echo $nfields ## alternatively, using bc for the arithmetic nfields=$(echo "${nfields}+1" | bc) ``` `grep -o ','` prints each match on its own line, so `wc -l` counts the commas; the number of fields is one more than that. Two questions the course leaves open here, worth sitting with before moving on: how could this syntax give the wrong answer (think about what a comma *inside* a quoted field does to this count), and how would you check that every line of the file has the same number of fields rather than trusting the last one? ### Mission 3 — was a package imported in any of the 5 most recently touched files? ```bash grep -l 'import requests' unit4-goodPractices.qmd # does this one file contain it? ls -tr *.qmd # all files, oldest to newest touch unit4-goodPractices.qmd # force it to be "recent", for demonstration ls -tr *.qmd | tail -n 5 ls -tr *.qmd | tail -n 5 | grep requests # wrong — see below ls -tr *.qmd | tail -n 5 | grep "unit4-goodPractices" # also just matching filenames ls -tr *.qmd | tail -n 5 | xargs grep 'import requests' ls -tr *.qmd | tail -n 5 | xargs grep -l 'import requests' ``` `man tail` shows it accepts a FILE or `stdin`; here it takes `stdin`, so it returns the last five *lines of the `ls` output* — five filenames — not the last five lines of any file named in that output. `man grep` likewise accepts a FILE or `stdin`, but piping the filenames straight into `grep` makes `grep` search those filenames as if they were the text to search, not open them as files. To make `grep` treat the piped names as FILE arguments, the filenames have to be converted from `stdin` into an argument list — that is what `xargs` does. An alternative to `xargs` is to use command substitution to embed the filenames directly as arguments: ```bash grep -l 'import requests' $(ls -tr *.R | tail -n 5) ``` ### Mission 4 — move the n most recently modified files, as a function Start from one concrete case, then generalize: ```bash ls -rt ~/Downloads | tail -n 5 mv "/accounts/vis/paciorek/Downloads/$(ls -rt \ /accounts/vis/paciorek/Downloads | tail -n 1)" ~/Desktop function mvlast() { mv "/accounts/vis/paciorek/Downloads/$(ls -rt \ /accounts/vis/paciorek/Downloads | tail -n 1)" $1 } ``` The full path is used instead of `~` because `~` can behave unreliably inside scripts, and the double quotes around the `$(...)` matter: without them, a filename containing a space would be split into two separate words and break the `mv`. An earlier version of this same example, run without the quotes, indeed only worked for filenames with no spaces in them. To move more than one file, wrap the same idea in a loop: ```bash function mvlast() { for ((i=1; i<=${1}; i++)); do mv "/accounts/vis/paciorek/Downloads/$(ls -rt \ /accounts/vis/paciorek/Downloads | tail -n 1)" ${2} done } ``` (If you only needed files from the current directory and none of their names had spaces, `tail -n ${1}` alone would replace the loop.) ### Mission 5 — reconstruct a project's dependencies from its source files The task: find every package imported anywhere in the course's `.qmd` files and write a `requirements.txt` that would let someone else recreate the environment. ```bash grep import *.qmd grep --no-filename import *.qmd grep --no-filename "^import" *.qmd grep --no-filename "^import " *.qmd grep --no-filename "^import " *.qmd | sort | uniq grep --no-filename "^import " *.qmd | cut -d'#' -f1 grep --no-filename "^import " *.qmd | cut -d'#' -f1 | sed "s/as .*//" grep --no-filename "^import " *.qmd | cut -d'#' -f1 | \ sed "s/as .*//" | sed "s/import //" > tmp.txt sed "s/,/\n/g" tmp.txt | sed "s/ //g" | sort | uniq | tee requirements.txt ## on a Mac, the newline in the sed replacement needs an extra escape: 's/,/\\\n/g' echo "There are $(wc -l requirements.txt | cut -d' ' -f1) unique packages we will install." ## on Linux, wc -l puts the count first; on a Mac it can be padded with leading ## spaces, so use: wc -l requirements.txt | tr -s ' ' | cut -d' ' -f2 pip install -r requirements.txt # or use Mamba/Conda ``` Each step narrows the noise: dropping filenames, anchoring `^import ` so a stray mention of "import" mid-line doesn't count, stripping trailing `# comment` text and `as alias`, splitting comma-separated imports onto their own lines, then deduplicating. This is not how you would actually solve dependency-tracking in practice — a package like R's `renv` or `packrat` exists precisely for this — the point is how quickly ordinary text tools compose into something fairly elaborate. The same technique, run over R source instead of Python, is exactly analogous: `grep --no-filename "^library" *.R`, followed by stripping `library(...)` down to the bare package name, then `Rscript -e "install.packages(...)"` at the end — the mechanism (filter, extract, deduplicate, act) doesn't care which language it's harvesting from. ### Mission 6 — find and kill a batch of runaway jobs Suppose a `for` loop in bash accidentally launched thirty background jobs and they need killing. ```bash cat > job.py << EOF import time time.sleep(1e5) EOF ## or: echo -e "import time\ntime.sleep(1e5)" > job.py nJobs=30 for (( i=1; i<=${nJobs}; i++ )); do python job.py > job-${i}.out & done # on Linux: ps -o pid,pcpu,pmem,user,cmd -C python ps -o pid,pcpu,pmem,user,cmd,start_time --sort=start_time -C python | tail -n 30 ps -o pid --sort=start_time -C python | tail -n ${nJobs} | xargs kill # on a Mac (no easy way to sort by start time): ps -o pid,pcpu,pmem,user,command | grep python ps -o pid,command | grep python | cut -d' ' -f1 | tail -n ${nJobs} | xargs kill ``` The `<< EOF ... EOF` construction is a *here document*: it feeds everything between the two `EOF` markers to the command as if it were typed at a prompt. `&` backgrounds each job so the loop doesn't block; `ps` with custom columns, sorted by start time, followed by `tail` and `xargs kill`, is how you find and kill only the newest batch. If the jobs were started all at once, their process IDs are often sequential, in which case brace expansion is a shortcut: `kill {871841..871870}`. ## Portability between Linux and Mac The same handful of gotchas recur across every one of the examples above, so it's worth collecting them: - GNU-specific flags exist that BSD (Mac) tools don't accept — `ls --all` and `ps --sort=start_time` both work on Linux and fail on MacOS. - `sed`'s replacement text needs an extra backslash for a literal newline on Mac (`'s/,/\\\n/g'`) compared to Linux (`'s/,/\n/g'`). - `wc -l`'s output is left-aligned on Linux but can come padded with leading spaces on Mac, which breaks a naive `cut -d' ' -f1` and needs `tr -s ' '` first to collapse the padding. - Sorting `ps` output by start time is straightforward on Linux (`--sort=start_time`) and has no clean equivalent on Mac. None of these change what the commands *mean* — only which flags exist — but they are exactly the kind of thing that silently breaks a script moved from one machine to another. ## Regular expressions Regular expressions ("regex") are a small domain-specific language for finding and manipulating patterns of characters. They are built into `grep`, `sed` and `awk`, and into scripting languages such as Python's `re` and R's `stringr`. Typical uses: extracting pieces of text, turning information found in text into variables, cleaning text into a uniform format, and treating a corpus of documents as data to be mined. The actual syntax — character classes, quantifiers, anchors, groups — is covered by an external tutorial the course assigns as reading rather than material presented in the unit itself, and the course returns to it again in a later unit when using Python's `re` package. What the unit does add on top of that reading is two things worth carrying forward on their own. **There is more than one dialect.** `man grep` distinguishes *basic* regular expressions (least functionality), *extended* regular expressions (the standard, and what the course's reference tutorial documents), and *Perl* regular expressions (most functionality). In `bash`, `grep -E` (or `egrep`) turns on extended syntax and `grep -P` turns on Perl syntax; Python's `re` module is "similar to" Perl syntax; R's `stringr` uses ICU regular expressions, which are themselves based on Perl. A pattern that behaves as expected in one of these can silently misbehave in another, purely because of which dialect it's being interpreted under. Deliberately out of scope for the course: callbacks, named groups, recursion, word boundaries, and lookaround assertions — all real regex features, just not needed for what the course does with them. **Build and debug a regex in pieces.** Because the syntax is so concise, treat a regex as its own small program: build it up component by component rather than writing the whole pattern at once, the same discipline you'd apply to any other code. The genuinely useful trick for debugging one is to use a tool that shows you *what actually matched* — `re.findall` in Python, `str_detect` in R's `stringr`, or the interactive site regex101.com — since, as with most kinds of coding, debugging a regex tends to take more time than writing it did in the first place. ## Exercises Rewritten from the course's own challenge set; not solved here. 1. Write a shell command that prints a sentence of the form "There are 8 occurrences of the word 'Belgium' in this file," where the number is computed from `cpds.csv`, not hard-coded. Then turn the command into a function that takes the filename and the word as arguments. 2. Using `RTADataSub.csv`: find the unique values of the fourth column, then automate checking whether any of those values are non-numeric (the pattern `[^0-9]` matches any character that is *not* a digit), so you don't have to scan the unique values by eye. Extend this to every field except the first, and have the code print its findings in a form someone who didn't write it could read. You may assume you know the number of fields in advance. 3. Using `cpds.csv`: find Belgium's minimum unemployment value (field 6) programmatically, and print it as "Belgium 6.2". Then store the unique country names in a variable, first stripping the surrounding quotation marks. Generalize the calculation to run for every country and print all the results to the screen — and then again, to write them to a file instead. 4. Using `RTADataSub.csv`, where a missing value is marked with an `x`: write out a new file with every row containing an `x` removed. Turn this into a function that also reports, to `stdout`, how many rows it removed (so the function can still be used in a pipeline), and then generalize the function so the caller supplies both the missing-value marker and the input filename. 5. Using `coop.txt`: rather than finding the state field's byte position by eye, use `grep` to search for a known state/country combination and print the byte offset of the match. Use that offset, computed programmatically, to drive the same `cut` extraction used in the first worked example. 6. A harder one. A CSV file has fields that themselves contain commas, once quoted: ``` 1,"America, United States of",45,96.1,"continental, coastal" 2,"France",33,807.1,"continental, coastal" ``` `cut` can't be used directly on this, because it has no idea the commas inside the quoted fields don't count as delimiters. Rewrite the file so it uses a different delimiter that isn't ambiguous in this way. At least one solution to this particular two-line example needs nothing more than plain string substitution — no regular expression required. 7. Regex challenge: work out the pattern needed to detect a number, whether integer- or real-valued. Start test-driven: write down the cases you want it to match, the cases that look similar but should not match, and the corner cases that are easy to get wrong before writing the pattern itself. ## Sources - **Fall 2025**, `units/unit3-bash.qmd` — the primary source for this chapter: shell basics, passing information between commands, all six worked "missions," the challenge set (§4.1–4.6), and the regular-expressions overview and challenge. berkeley-stat243, CC BY 4.0. - **Fall 2024**, `units/unit3-bash.qmd` — the same unit one year earlier, nearly identical text; used to confirm which details (e.g. the sequential-PID `kill {a..b}` shortcut, the extra "Danger" note on `ls --all`) were added between the two years rather than dropped. berkeley-stat243, CC BY 4.0. - **Fall 2021** (`stat243-fall-2021`), `units/unit3-bash.pdf` — an earlier version of the same unit, run with R instead of Python: source of the R-based variant of Mission 5, the unquoted `mvlast` bug fixed in later years, and the "New Zealand" quoting detail in the challenge set. This file is a model's reconstruction of a PDF with no text layer, and is flagged by its own conversion banner as paraphrased and not independently citable; used here only for details corroborated by the plainer Fall 2024/2025 markdown. berkeley-stat243, CC0-1.0. - **Not used**: `fall-2026/units/unit3-goodPractices/*` was supplied as input but covers a different topic — coding style, debugging with `pdb`, and reproducible research — that the course moved into the "unit 3" slot in that year. It has no bash-shell content and does not belong in a chapter on shell basics. - **Referred to by the lecture but not supplied**, and so not reproduced here: the course's own bash shell tutorial (`tutorial-using-bash`, mirrored at both `berkeley-scf.github.io` and `computing.stat.berkeley.edu`), which carries the actual command syntax, the "Managing Processes" material behind Mission 6, and the full regular-expression reference; Newham and Rosenblatt, *Learning the bash Shell*, 2nd ed.; Duncan Temple Lang's regex tutorial; §§9.9 and 11 of Paul Murrell's *Introduction to Data Technologies*; the `stringr` regex cheatsheet; and regex101.com.
